subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON MONDAY, APRIL 25

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext:
I should like to move, as provided by the notice which appears on today's order paper under government notices of motions:
That on Monday, the 25th April instant, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except questions and notices of motions for the production of papers.
The purpose of this motion is to proceed as rapidly as possible with the debate on the budget. In view of the long list of interesting speeches which have been made on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, it is hoped that the debate on the budget may be brief. I trust that we may now have the co-operation of the house in bringing the debate to a close today, or at the latest tomorrow, so that we may get into committee on the resolutions.
Judging from the tone of the debate thus far, I have been under the impression that everything in these resolutions was looked upon as good, and that if there was any criticism of them it was that there were not more of them, or that they did not go far enough. It would seem that the general feeling was that what is there is quite properly there, although some hon. members felt that there might have been more. If it suits the convenience of the house, we should like to get on with the debate as soon as possible.
When we adjourned for the Easter recess, the Minister of Public Works announced that the house would be asked to consider the resolution of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) having to do with an amendment to

Business of the House
the Judges Act to provide for a possible increase in the number of judges in the province of Quebec. Legislation to this end has been passed by the Quebec legislature, but has not yet been proclaimed. It is felt by many that serious delays are occasioned by the fact that there is more work to do than the present number of judges can take care of, and that it might be desirable to have the Judges Act in such shape that an early appointment of additional judges can be made if and when the government of Quebec proclaims the provincial legislation to which I have referred. To proceed with this resolution would require the unanimous consent of the house, because it is only at the stage where His Excellency's acquiescence would be declared; normally it could not come up for consideration until the next sitting. If there were objection to its being considered today, of course the objection would have to prevail.
There is also on the order paper a resolution dealing with family allowances; it proposes that the period of waiting required of children coming into the country be reduced from three years to one year, and provides for the elimination of the decrease in scale in family allowances resulting from the number of children in the family. This seems to be something which most parties in this house advocate; therefore it may be that the resolution can be expeditiously disposed of so that the bill founded on it could be brought down, and any debate that might arise on the principle of the sufficiency or insufficiency of the measure proposed by the government could take place on the bill. However, the government would not care to insist upon this, because it was not announced before the house rose for the Easter recess. The purpose of this motion is to make way for the budget debate. If these two measures which I have mentioned can be expeditiously disposed of, it will further the progress of their consideration at later stages.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext:
While I think the house will agree with the motion, I want to say again it is regrettable that in recent sessions of parliament private members' resolutions have not been reached. There are on the order paper a number of private members' resolutions which are of importance to their constituencies and to the country generally. It is true that in the debate on the address and on the budget we have an opportunity to debate some of these matters. But many hon. members have exhausted their right to speak in these two debates, and they would like the opportunity to deal with such matters, for example, as irrigation, or the coal mining industry and a national fuel policy, which are the subject matter of a IMr. St. Laurent.]
motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr Gillis).
Before the war we used to have debates on private members' resolutions which I think were very useful. Over the past few years we have been deprived of that opportunity-with our own consent, incidentally, always; but it is regrettable that this has been done again at this session. The Prime Minister said earlier in the session that opportunities would be given later for hon. members to discuss their resolutions, but on the first day of our meeting after the Easter recess we have this motion of the Prime Minister which again prevents the consideration of private members' resolutions. It is wise that we should go on with the business of the house. Apparently there is a good deal of uncertainty in the house and throughout the country as to how long this session will continue. In spite of that uncertainty, we should endeavour to deal with some of these matters which are of importance to private members, who have few opportunities of discussing them.
While I am not opposing the motion now before the house, I offer this protest and ask that private members' days be not interfered with again during this session.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext:
There are two things I should like to say. First of all I want to support the request made by my leader that, if the session goes on, further private members' days be not again taken away. I remind the Prime Minister that on March 25 the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked if we would be having private members' days, and the Prime Minister replied that after Monday-the Monday then following-there would be nothing to interfere with the application of the standing orders. Since that statement was made, there have been three occasions on which the application of the standing orders would have provided a private members' day; we had only one of them, and now the opportunity is again taken away by this motion. The Prime Minister should indicate today what the intention of the government is with respect to Wednesday of this week, Monday of next week and Wednesday of next week, and so on-if we are still here. Perhaps the Prime Minister would take advantage of this opportunity to tell us whether or not we shall still be here.
The other matter which I should like to draw to the Prime Minister's attention is this. Each time a motion of this kind has been passed by the house we seem to have omitted the calling of the orders of the day. That is perfectly understandable; today, for instance, we pass a motion calling for questions, and then for government orders which appear at the back of the order paper; and perhaps

inadvertently-or it may be because Mr. Speaker feels it should be done that way-the orders of the day have not been called. I submit that the phrase "orders of the day" applies not only to the page on which that heading appears, but also to all subsequent pages.
If this motion passes, in view of the fact that many of us have questions to ask today, will it be understood that at some stage of this afternoon's proceedings "orders of the day" will be called?

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON MONDAY, APRIL 25
speechtext: I think it would be the desire of hon. members to have the orders of the day called before proceeding with the matters which would come under the standing orders.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
that the house go into committee this day to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Judges Act, 1946, to authorize the governor in council to increase the number of judges of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec by not more than six judges.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: This is the resolution 1 mentioned when I moved that government orders be taken into consideration today. If I have the unanimous consent I would ask that instead of going into committee at the next sitting, the house go into committee on the resolution today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I think there is very little that can be added to the remarks which were made by the Prime Minister when the house was discussing the advisability of proceeding with this item at today's sitting. There is a serious shortage of judges in Quebec, particularly in Montreal-so much so that a large number of cases have been piled up awaiting consideration by the courts. As the Prime Minister said, the Quebec legislature, in pursuance of their authority to create the position of judge, have passed a law providing for additional judges of the superior court of that province. That law is subject to proclamation, and the proclamation has not yet been made. The purpose of the bill, to which the resolution leads, is to enable us, in the event of the provincial law being proclaimed, to appoint these judges in order that there will be a sufficient staff in the province of Quebec to reduce the arrears, and to carry on the administration of justice and the hearing of cases in the way in which it should be done.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
In view of the fact that a recommendation for an increase in the number of the judiciary has

been made, and in view of the accumulation of work to which my hon. friend, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), has referred, there can be no objection to this resolution. There are a few words, however, that I should like to say as to the judiciary, and as to what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said this afternoon when asked by my friend, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), whether or not orders in council passed since the first of July last would be tabled before dissolution. I was surprised at the answer given by the Prime Minister. I wish to deal with the question of administrative law and also with the matter of judicial appointments, because we have arrived at a point where the work of the judiciary of the country has been encroached upon in large measure by the semi-judicial decisions of bureaucrats in their various offices. The Prime Minister indicated that the house could not expect to have his assurance-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows perfectly well that his remarks are not relevant to the motion that is before the house. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I have not finished.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon. member to see that his remarks are relevant to the motion before the house, which is to present a bill to amend the Judges Act so as to authorize the governor in council to increase the number of judges of the superior court of the province of Quebec by not more than six. I do not think such a motion has anything to do with orders in council.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with all the respect that I can command I want to tell you that I think, with deference, that the question as to whether or not extra judges should be appointed brings up for consideration the fact that most of their functions today are exercised and executed by administrative bodies. I intended to point out that this is a good move. The government apparently has decided that it is going to come to the end of administrative law with judicial decisions rendered by administrative bodies from which citizens are denied the right of appeal, and intends to restore the judiciary of the country as far as possible so that it will discharge its judicial function.
I find that there has been a substantial increase in the number of judges during the years. I had a return made last year for the purpose of ascertaining the situation. I found that since 1921 there had been appointed seventy-five court of appeal judges, of whom all but eight were appointed by a Liberal gov-
Judges Act
ernment. In supreme and superior courts there had been 166 appointments, of which all but thirty had been made by Liberal governments.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
I cannot quite understand the applause from the other side of the house.
I never knew before that political fitness was a qualification for judicial appointment. Of the 211 county or district court judges appointed, all but twenty-three were appointed by a Liberal government. I am glad to see the increase in the number of judges for the purpose of taking up the slack, because a strong judiciary is needed in Canada to maintain the rights of individuals against the invasions of bureaucracy so characteristic of this government.
As a matter of fact, to a very large extent today-and I am sure that the Prime Minister will agree with this-bureaucracy exercises judicial functions without the right of appeal to the courts. Too often appeals are decided on administrative matters not by the courts but by ministers whose decisions are governed by departmental officials and departmental files. The result is that, unless there is an appeal to the courts, the individual feels that he has not secured justice when and if orders are made against him. I should like to have an assurance from the minister that courts of bureaucracy will be reduced, if not entirely eliminated, because in those courts decisions are made in which prejudice too often takes the place of judicial wisdom, and suspicion and hearsay are accepted as evidence.
With the increase of six judges in the judiciary of the province of Quebec, with the ample increases that have taken place in recent years, and with the higher salaries that are now being paid to judges as a result of which the very best men can be mobilized, I should like to see the Minister of Justice give the lead in putting an end to bureaucratic decisions, an end to control by Ottawa rather than by law.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows perfectly well that the question before the house is a motion to present a bill to amend the Judges Act to authorize the governor in council to increase the number of judges of the superior court of the province of Quebec by not more than six. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: If the hon. member has finished I should like to say that I do not intend to allow these broad allegations to go unchallenged. The hon. member knows that he has been setting up men of straw for the purpose of knocking them down.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Let him finish his speech.

Judges Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I beg your pardon; I thought the hon. member had finished.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I was trying to show how necessary it was to have an increase.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Support the measure.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Yes, support the measure, absolutely. I want to point out why it should be supported, why it is necessary to restore to the judiciary many of the powers that have been filched from it by this administration. That is the point I am making. The Prime Minister has become suddenly aroused. I can understand that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: You are a good enough lawyer to understand that anyone listening to you would become aroused.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: This is a very touchy point. The Prime Minister becomes aroused, a former president of the Canadian Bar Association, who often, in that capacity, averred the very things I am stating today, and said that it was necessary to restore to the courts their customary responsibility under our constitution. Surely there is no reason for the Prime Minister to become so aroused, so nettled, so disturbed. All I have asked is that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson)-who is not responsible for these things, because he has been minister only a short while-see that the courts have restored to them the protection of the rights of the individual in this country as against administrative orders, often unjust and discriminatory, which deny to the individual that justice which should be assured to him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: The hon. member has suggested that I became aroused. I did become aroused on hearing a lawyer make these general statements, so utterly strange and so utterly removed from the facts, and without trying to bring forward any facts to support his general statement. Over the years there has been an administrative tribunal which was set up by the government in power in 1917 and which made final decisions as to the assessment of income tax against Canadian taxpayers.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Oh, you have heard about income tax? I have not spoken about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
That has been removed, and a judicial board has been set up to which an appeal may be taken by anyone who feels himself aggrieved in the fixing of his taxes. When the hon. member talks about other bureaucratic courts I do not know what he is referring to. He may have in mind the fact that in the administration of rental controls, which the provincial jurisdictions have refused to take on, there are special courts to decide whether exceptions can be made to
fMr. Graydon.]
the general application of those rules. But to try to create the impression that this country is not governed by the rule of law applied by courts of justice is to make an imputation which our brand of democracy does not warrant.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to say what allocation will be made of the judges as between districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
No, not altogether, because in the main that will depend upon the terms of the provincial enactment creating the vacancies. As my hon. friend is well aware, it is within the provincial authority to set up the courts and create the judicial vacancies, and within our authority to fill them; and we will fill those vacancies created by the provincial act in the form in which it is finally proclaimed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I have just one question to ask the Minister of Justice; perchance he has answered it already, but there has been a bit of confusion here this afternoon. If this bill passes are any further steps necessary before the appointment of the additional judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Yes, indeed. As I indicated in my previous remarks, under the British North America Act authority to create the courts and to create these judicial vacancies rests with the provincial government. The legislature of Quebec has passed a law creating these vacancies, but that law does not come into force until it is proclaimed. Before these vacancies can be filled the provincial law has to be proclaimed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Then what we are doing to the government of Quebec is somewhat similar to what the legislature of Manitoba has done to this government in the matter of coarse grains; that is, we are forcing their hands?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

Not at all. We are placing ourselves in the position that we will be able to fill the vacancies created in Quebec when the proclamation is issued. If we did not pass this legislation now and the provincial law should be proclaimed in August, let us

say, we would have to wait until this house met again before we could fill the vacancies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: If I may add just a word here, the Quebec law authorizes the lieutenant governor in council to increase the number of judges by not more than six. That is why there is provision here that the additional number for whom salaries will be provided will be fixed by the governor in council here in Ottawa, because until that law is proclaimed we do not know whether it will be for three, four, five or six. We will have to make our order in council comply with the terms of the proclamation issued by the government of Quebec.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: In other words when this legislation has been passed the necessary provincial and federal legislation will have been completed. After that there will have to be the proclamation by the provincial government and action taken by the federal governor in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Right.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Has there been any indication from the attorney general of Quebec as to whether or not there is going to be immediate proclamation? Has any representation been made along that line, or any indication given?

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I have discussed this matter in a general way with the attorney general of Quebec and he agrees that there is necessity for these appointments, but I do not think it would be correct to say that he has given any explicit undertaking about the immediate proclamation of the provincial act.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Aside from any explicit undertaking, has there been any indication as to when the proclamation will be issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: No.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Are we here asking for the appointment of judges, when the final disposition of the matter is left with the province; and would that be so if they signified to this government that they actually needed twelve judges to carry out the judicial work in that province?

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Read the bill.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I am not a Rhodes scholar, but in a brief question I can put a great deal more common sense than you can. We have heard from you so many times that we are sick of you. You are not the Minister of Justice, and never will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
To reply to my hon. friend's question, the fact is that at the present time there are between 4,500 and 5,000 cases of arrears waiting to be heard in the superior
Judges Act
court of Quebec. There is no question at all about the necessity for additional judges. The only way in which they can be appointed by this government is by the prior creation of the vacancies by the provincial legislatures in accordance with their constitutional powers under the British North America Act. The passage by the Quebec legislature of the act which is now on their statute books, unproclaimed, is an indication or an admission that there is a need for more judges. The purpose of the present bill is an exceedingly simple one. We want to put this government in the position that, as soon as that provincial law has been proclaimed, we shall be able, without delay, to fill these vacancies which need so badly to be filled.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: The reply given by the minister is, I must say, enlightening to many laymen in this house. There are few who know everything about the law: those who interfere and interrupt unnecessarily in this house never go far in the profession.

maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: The minister has just told us that there are some 5,000 cases waiting to be heard. If that is the case, it would certainly appear that the necessity for these additional judges is urgent. Can the minister tell the committee how long these cases have been awaiting hearing and why these people who are going to law in order to get justice have been compelled to wait over the past year? Surely this situation did not arise overnight. It seems odd that this power had not been asked for at least a year or two ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: JUDGES ACT, 1945 PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES OF SUPERIOR COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend's interjection, I might point out that the present situation speaks eloquently for itself. We are asking for this authority from the House of Commons in advance of the time at which it is necessary for us to exercise it. I do not want to repeat myself too often but, as I pointed out before, the authority for the creation of the courts and of judicial vacancies rests with the provincial legislature. In reply to the other part of my hon. friend's question, I would hazard the guess that a large number of these cases may have been awaiting trial for perhaps somewhere between one and a half and two years. I think that is a fairly conservative statement. We have had cognizance of the situation, but may I point out that it is impossible for us to fill a vacancy which does not exist; the only authority to create a vacancy rests with the provincial legislature.

It

We are all for family allowances; we could not be otherwise. But our suggestion is that a great deal of the money being used for social services can come from its original source rather than from the taxpayers. I recognize the fact that an election is to be held soon, and I am beginning to think that we should have them more often. Perhaps if we did the people of Canada would receive these benefits more frequently than they do. It seems to me that about the only time they can expect promise of benefits is when an election is on the horizon.
Once again in respect of these measures connected with social services, may I offer the warning that if we continue to finance them at the expense of the taxpayers we will eventually come under the tyranny of the supreme state. No one could be happier than I as the minister in charge of this measure at the words expressed by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray don). I take it that his words represent the conviction and faith of the party of which he is so distinguished a member. But I need only point out at the outset that if that is the case, and I would suspect from what he says that it is, it represents in spite of what may be said to the contrary a change of heart on the part of a goodly number of hon. gentlemen in this house.
The bill which will be introduced proposes to do two things: first, to eliminate that provision in the act which calls for reduc-
Family Allowances Act tions to be made from the total family allowance cheque to any family which has five or more children and, second, to reduce, from three years to one year, the waiting period in respect of families recently arrived in Canada and lacking residence or domicile in this country.
The act as it presently stands requires certain deductions to be made from family allowances paid to families of five or more children in the following amounts:
$1 deduction for the fifth child:
$2 deduction for the sixth child:
$2 deduction for the seventh child;
$3 deduction for the eighth and each subsequent child.
Those deductions will be done away with under the amending bill which we seek to have made part of the law of our country. When the bill becomes law the scale of payments will be as follows:
$5 for each child under 6 years of age;
$6 for each child over 6 and under 10 years of age;
$7 for each child over 10 and under 13 years of age;
$8 for each child over 13 and under 16 years of age.
There will be no deduction on account of the size of the family. The measure of which these particular amendments will form an integral part represents, I think, the greatest single act of social reform introduced by any country in the last quarter century. If anyone wants to question that statement all he need do is to read the observations made by the present prime minister of the United Kingdom when he was speaking in Liverpool on May 14, 1946.
This act will have resulted in the distribution by the end of May of $1,000 million to almost 1,800,000 families representing some four million children. Since 1945, as a result of this measure, there has come to these children an added incentive, an opportunity for improved education through being able to stay at school longer. This measure has meant for them improved medical attention, improvement in clothing, improvement in nutrition, to such an extent that throughout this country recent Gallup polls have shown that in the judgment of the Canadian people this measure is one of the great acts of social reform of our time.
Why do I say that? I say that because we want to make sure that this present Family Allowances Act of ours shall remain as part of the statute law of this country. As I hope to show before I shall have taken my seat, there is considerable reason for feeling that if certain people get into power in this country that might not be the case. That is a tremendous figure which represents a substantial redistribution of the nation's wealth. It represents a transfer of purchasing power from those who are able to share their good fortune with the future citizens of our country who, because of the financial situation of their parents, are unable to enjoy the same measure of advantage.
I do not think anyone will deny the value of this achievement to date when he realizes that under the Family Allowances Act some $200 million is distributed every year at a cost of less than $4 million. I think it will be generally recognized that that is no mean achievement from the administrative point of view, apart altogether from the very substantial benefits that it brings to so many of our people. Surely those vast sums of the national wealth could not be invested in a worthier cause than the welfare of the nation's children. One can think of the benefits that flow from this expenditure on our children in the way of better health, better medical attention, better school attendance and better food and clothing, especially for our less prosperous families.
I am sure that if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) were in his seat today he would say as a former minister of education in the province of Ontario, as indeed all ministers of education in all of our provinces can attest, that since the introduction of family allowances school attendance figures in our country are, and have been since 1945, at

The family allowance scheme has all the earmarks of a political bribe.

He said the plan costing $200 million would increase peacetime taxes by 50 per cent. As an alternative he proposed the removal of the ceiling on low wages and easing of income tax levies on low wage groups.

About a year ago, as the minister will recall, I had occasion to speak on this question in the house, and at that time I suggested two particular changes in the Family Allowances Act, one of which I see is to be embodied in this legislation. I refer to the waiting period for newcomers to this country, which is to be reduced from three years to one year. I believe that is an admirable step, for I am sure everyone will agree that for those coming to this country to make a living the first few years are bound to be the very hardest, and the assistance given by this measure will be deeply appreciated. My other request was that the age limit be extended upward in the case of children continuing to go to school, in order that the children of parents in moderate circumstances might be able to get a better education in the higher schools.
I might add that in the view of those who belong to this group this is a form of social security, and I am happy to say that we are beginning to see the fruits of the labour of many of those who formed this party in the first instance. I believe it is a matter of history that the late J. S. Woodsworth was recognized in Canada as a crusader for social security, while I believe Miss Macphail, who formerly sat in this house and who now sits in another place, was one of the first to mention family allowances here. So we look at this matter from that point of view, because we believe there is a difference in the philosophy of various parties on the question of social security. Before the measure passes I should like to say a word or two. Family allowances are sound in that they aim to increase the purchasing power in the hands of the public. It is high time that all people concerned with public life in Canada and elsewhere came to realize that there is a progressive shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people because of the development of machines. Means must be adopted to increase that purchasing power which has been lost by reason of machines. Family allowances are one of the means which must be adopted at least while we pursue the present financial system.
Family allowances aim to help our children to enjoy a higher standard of food, clothing, shelter, health and education, and in that respect they are sound. Family allowances are becoming more and more absolutely necessary as people are more and more impoverished by taxation, by unemployment and by decreasing purchasing power in their hands.
I find many people today whom I meet on the streets, in the trains and elsewhere wondering why it is that since our dear old dads and our dear old granddads did not have these "highfalutin" social services we must have them. The great trouble with all such people who ask such questions is this, they just do not know what is happening to the economy of these times as a result of machines, increased production and displacement of men. We must view all matters such as these family allowances in the light of what is hap-

pening in that regard. For the same reasons we must have more and more of other kinds of social services, larger old age pensions, larger health assistance measures, and the like. I think it would be neglectful on our parts if we failed once more this year to bring these matters forcibly to the attention of the house and of the country, and that there is going on in the body economic of every nation in the world a change as a result of the use of machines and power. Since the granting of the family allowance must be based upon need, I suggest that generally speaking the need of those who have just arrived here from other countries is even greater than that of those who may have been here for one year or more. I have had some experience with displaced persons, the parents of large families of small children who, largely owing to faulty government screening, were brought out here as trained mechanics. After a certain time it was discovered that they were not able to do the things they said they could do; and I do not think anyone would blame them for attempting to escape from the conditions under which they were living by saying anything that would help them better their condition. However that may be, and irrespective of whose fault it may have been, they found themselves in this country, out of work and in some cases without having put in the necessary number of days to qualify for unemployment insurance.
In such cases it seems to me rather hard on the municipalities to have to put up money for the relief of these people who were supposed to be accurately screened by the government before being brought here and turned loose-and I use those words advisedly -to fend for themselves. From that point

on the dominion government assumes no responsibility. I know of one case, of a woman who was sent out to work on a farm. As far as I could see she was a good worker and a pleasant person, but she did not get along with the people to whom she was sent. The farmer for whom she was working brought her into a little prairie town, dumped her off on the wooden sidewalk and there she was, without sufficient knowledge of the English language to make her situation known. She was looked after by some kindly person and the matter was fixed up, but she did not know what to do or where to go.
So in this connection I think the government has shown laxity in two respects. In the first place I do not think they follow up these cases sufficiently in order to see that these people are satisfactorily placed. In the second place, as I said in the beginning, I see no reason why it would not be a good investment for the people of this country to give the family allowance to these displaced persons immediately upon their arrival in Canada. I believe it would avoid a great deal of grief later on; and if the dominion government assumed that responsibility the local people would not have to assume other responsibilities later on. I would be interested to hear some comment from the minister on that one point, as to why family allowances are not paid to these people immediately they land in this country. They are potential Canadian citizens. Speaking metaphorically I think it would start them off with a better taste in their mouth; and speaking literally I think it would put more taste in the mouths of the children if they were given this allowance immediately upon their arrival, as a right and not as charity. Would the minister comment upon that point?

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the budget I must confess that this is a rather novel experience for me, because in the nine years I have been in parliament I have never taken part in a budget debate. The reason is quite simple; I have so thoroughly approved of the sequence of budgets brought down by Mr. Ilsley and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that I have seen no reason to prolong the debate merely to voice my approval.
This budget, however, is so exceptional that I think I should at least express the gratification of my constituents at the announcement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It is not just in my constituency, of course, for from British Columbia to Newfoundland, Canadians have hailed it as the greatest budget in our history. The daily press of the country made it the news of the year in their front pages the day after it was delivered and in their editorial columns they lauded it. I need not weary the house by quoting excerpts of their praise, because all hon. members are familiar with it. Still keener and more impartial has been the praise from other lands, praise untinged by the political bias which might be found in Canadian commentators.
Senator George, who is the democratic chairman of the United States senate finance committee, thought so highly of the minister's speech that he placed it on the United States senate record and urged the United States administration

and this is a democratic senator-to follow a similar program or, he emphasized, there would be a flight of United States capital to the security of Canada. Barron's, the great United States financial weekly, devoted almost their full front page to an analysis of the Canadian budget, holding it up as a model for the United States government to follow and describing


Canada as "O blessed land." I do not intend to put all of this on the record but I think there are two paragraphs which are so significant of United States reaction that I should mention them:
Furthermore, lest anybody think the Canadians economized on the war and allowed others to do the sacrificing, let us remember that Canada contributed to the war effort of the United Kingdom gifts of goods and arms amounting to more than $1 billion annually. Counting in other contributions by Canada, the aggregate lend-lease outlay of that country has been fully proportionate to ours.
The Liberal party in Canada certainly has done well by the people. They have come through a long period of hardships and restrictions in a magnificent manner. Now that the post-war boom is waning, they are in a position to give themselves a large dose of tax relief, a major stimulant to both consumption and new investment.
Then this long article concludes by suggesting that President Truman should give his financial advisers an educational trip and send them up to Ottawa to find out from the Minister of Finance how it is done. These objective remarks from a foreign land are certainly in accord with the sentiments of the Canadian people. I might well ask at this time: What other country in the world today would not have welcomed a budget such as ours? I am quite sure that the British people turned envious eyes westward on the night of April 6 when they heard the bad news in their budget.
Despite this tremendous wave of approval, however, there are members in this house who have been assigned by their parties to find fault with and criticize this budget- which is a perfectly proper democratic procedure. Indeed, in the days before this administration took office, the fiery, sweeping all-out attacks of the opposition financial critics were almost as important as the budget itself.
Those of us who were in the house on the day of March 31, however, will recall how different was the scene that night. The financial critic of the opposition rose to his task and made a delightfully delivered speech, filled with amusing anecdotes and nicely turned phrases-the very picture of a scholar and a gentleman going through the motions of opposing a budget which he knew in his heart was a good budget, and one which had been enthusiastically welcomed by the Canadian people. The house that day accepted his speech in the very temper in which it was given, because I have never seen the house so jovial and happily relaxed-Liberal members and opposition members alike heartily applauding his pleasant sallies. The financial critics of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit group who followed him spoke in similar vein, their main theme being that if they had

been the government they would have done the same thing a little sooner.
Just for fear that I am being a trifle partisan in my approach, because of my own appreciation of the budget and because of my close connection with the Minister of Finance, I will be objective and show how the national press reacted to the efforts of the financial critics. In days gone by the scathing slashing attacks of the financial critics always made the headlines. Let me, therefore, tell you how the largest paper in each of the four principal cities of Canada featured the speeches of the three financial critics in their issues of April 1: The Montreal Star, one-third of a column, on page 4; the Toronto Star, no mention anywhere; the Winnipeg Free Press, no mention anywhere; the Vancouver Sun, one-third of a column on page 30. To me that is the best indication of the ineffectualness, not of the members themselves-because they are all able parliamentarians-but of the ineffectualness of their critical efforts. The fault was not theirs. The story of course is that the budget was so good a budget that there was really nothing to criticize. Nevertheless, I feel that I should make some comments on some of the statements made by the principal financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell).
First and foremost was his comment that the budget was a political bribe, followed almost immediately by the naive observation that the Liberals had increased the income tax exemption to only $1,000 and $2,000 while the Progressive Conservatives had promised $1,250 and $2,500. The minister at that time aptly interjected the following remark:
Did I hear a reference to bribery a short time ago?
Since the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario did not explain the difference, perhaps I should. A Liberal promise carried out is regarded by the Tories as bribery, while a Tory promise unfulfilled is regarded by the people of Canada as just their customary fraud. This criticism, of course, points out the one thing which is really wrong with this budget-"it is fair to the people of Canada but it is unfair to the Tory party." However, while I am on this point I want to go a little bit further. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario once again dragged out and once again misquoted a remark made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce some years ago. It will be found at page 2251 of Hansard for 1945. Here is the quotation:
I call the attention of my hon. friend-
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.
-to the fact that we are dealing with an over-all bill for some $1,365 million ... X daresay my hon.
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair friend could cut a million dollars from this amount; but a million dollars from the war appropriation bill would not be a very important matter.
Now it is readily figured that a million dollars on an item of $1,365 million is less than seven one-hundredths of one per cent- surely remarkably little leeway on an estimate of expenditure. The Auditor General told us in committee just before the Easter recess that he would regard a leeway of one per cent on ordinary departmental estimates as extraordinarily close.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario however twists this statement around, after three years, as reported on page 2181 of Hansard of 1949, to this:
Yes, said Mr. Howe, we could have saved a million dollars, but what is a million dollars?
Bad though this twisting may be, now let us look at the speech of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario in this regard. In advocating the adoption of the Tory scale of exemption, $1,250 and $2,500, he used this priceless phrase:
As far as I can estimate from the figures I have, that would not have cost very much.
The figures are easily obtainable from the Department of Finance and as he is the chief financial critic of the Conservative party, I presume he did get these figures and study them. These figures show that the extra cost -the "not very much" of the hon. member's speech-is the trifling little sum of $140 million or 23 [DOT] 7 per cent of our present income tax collection. I am sure this house will now agree that whatever laurels the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) won for his casual reference to one million dollars in the war appropriations estimate must now pass to the brow of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario for his careful and studied classification of the sum of $140 million as "not very much."
However, before I leave this question of personal exemptions, I should like to make one observation. The phrase $1,000 and $2,000 rolls off our tongue so easily that we tend to forget that the actual exemptions for the class of people that this government wants most to help-married people with children-are actually far higher. A married couple with children receives an exemption of $150 for each child receiving family allowance or $400 if the child is dependent but does not receive family allowance. In the former case, however, the effect of family allowances must be considered because of the change in our income tax structure which was made to accommodate the payment of family allowances to everyone. That is the point which was raised by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) a moment ago. When family allowances were
2554	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair first brought in it will be recalled that they were paid to everyone as of right below $1,500, but between $1,500 and $3,000 a sliding scale of recovery was effected through a change in the income tax rates. Above $3,000 we took all the family allowances back through income tax. This method of payment aroused the suggestion that there was a means test about family allowances, and it also made it very difficult for the Department of National Revenue to administer collections, and costly too. Therefore family allowances were later made payable to everyone irrespective of income, and the actual tax rates were again changed to effect the same recovery from people of higher incomes. Therefore the true limit of income tax exemption for the family group is where the income tax paid by that group is equal to the family allowances received. The Department of Finance has worked this out as follows: for a family with one child, $2,630; for a family with two children, $3,260; for a family with three children, $3,838; for a family with four children, $4,412; and for a family with five children, $4,960. Hon. members will therefore see that actually our real exemptions are pretty close to the United States exemptions of $600 per child, and combined with our husband and wife exemptions they make our income tax exemptions the highest in the world.
Second only to the cut in personal income tax, as far as the general public is concerned, has been the removal or reduction of a wide range of sales and excise taxes. The reclassification of a great number of varying rates, some at manufacturers' level and some at retail level, will be welcomed for three main reasons. First and most obvious, it has brought an immediate reduction in the price of most of these items. Second, it has greatly simplified our excise tax structure by dividing it into just four main groups today: (1) the bulk of food and construction items on which neither sales tax nor excise tax is paid; (2) a large range of goods not in the luxury or nonessential class, on which only a sales tax of 8 per cent is levied, clothing and household furnishings for example; (3) a large range of goods such as cars, radios, phonographs, jewelry, furs, cosmetics, luggage, on which sales tax and 10 per cent excise tax is levied: (4) tobacco and liquor on which the traditionally high rate is levied. This simplification of categories will make them more easily understood by the public, and easier to administer by the Department of National Revenue. This classification also shows what is generally not understood, namely, that these taxes are in a measure progressive, since the greater the family's income the more its purchases will be in the higher and more heavily taxed groups.

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair
The truth is, of course, that the money is the taxpayers' money, collected to pay for services to them by both the federal and provincial governments. When Premier Hart signed this agreement it was hailed as a great thing for British Columbia, and I particularly remember Mr. Anscomb, Progressive Conservative leader in British Columbia, who was Mr. Hart's right hand man at the time, took good care to get his share of the credit for this splendid deal.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) last year, when he was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, had a careful study made by that department of just what federal services to British Columbia do cost. Since the hon. member for Kamloops used last year's figures, perhaps it would be interesting for hon. members to see what this statement contains. The statement is short, but I do not intend to read it all. It shows that the actual total taken from British Columbia in direct and indirect taxation last year amounted to $187,223,000 whereas the actual amount spent by the federal government in British Columbia through direct payments to the provincial government, direct payments to or on behalf of individual residents of the province, interest paid on Dominion of Canada bonds, major expenditures by government departments or agencies within the province, the proportional share of (a) subsidies paid under price control regulations and (b) dominion government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, and partial estimates of expenditures financed with moneys advanced by way of loans, totaled $220 million. That makes $187,223,000 as against $220 million.
If there is any interest in this table I shall be only too glad to have it included in my speech, so far as the details are concerned.

No account has been taken of the more general types of budgetary expenditures which are made for the benefit of the country as a whole, and which are of course of direct benefit to British Columbia as to all other provinces. Included in this category are the expenses of the central legislative body and of the financial and administrative departments of Ottawa, the services of such departments as National Health and Welfare, National Defence, External Affairs, Reconstruction and Supply, Trade and Commerce, and research activities of the National Research Council and other bodies, etc. All these services are of direct benefit to the residents of British Columbia and should not properly be omitted from consideration in any discussion of the benefits received by British Columbia in return for tax revenues collected there.
However, the hon. member for Kamloops might regard the Minister of Fisheries as a prejudiced witness. Therefore let me quote Premier Johnson, the leader of the provincial government, which, according to the hon. member, is so badly treated by this government-a government, incidentally, which this year has a budget of over $92 million for a million people.
In the legislature of British Columbia Mr. Harold Winch, leader of the opposition and C.C.F. leader, made a speech in a vein similar to that of the hon. member for Kamloops, which occasioned a debate. The Vancouver Province of Saturday, March 12, reported this debate as follows:
Mr. Johnson said he had done all in his power to press for the inauguration of a dominion contributory superannuation scheme.
"If we had had agreements from all of the provinces, the social security measures would have been implemented before now."
The Premier declared he was not concerned with the political aspects of dominion-provincial relations, but he believed "the smartest thing this government ever did was to enter into the agreement along with six other provinces."
Now, the hon. member for Kamloops might regard Mr. Johnson as prejudiced, since he is head of the Liberal party in B.C. Therefore let us quote Mr. Anscomb, leader of the Progressive Conservatives in B.C., in this same connection, as reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 12, page 3:
Mr. Winch insisted the government must start now studying the effects of the enormous income taxes taken out of British Columbia in relation to what the dominion gives back. (He estimated the rates at $6 to $1.)
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair
Mr. Anscomb insisted the finance department is studying it continually.
But he said British Columbia has made an agreement and will stick to it.
"The facts are now, however, that the benefits we are getting from Canada's new financial system far outweigh the .$140 or $150 million the people of this province pay in federal taxes.
He explained how the dominion, with its big taxation powers, is able to control credits and regulate overseas markets. British Columbia on its own could never finance the overseas purchases of lumber, for instance, like the dominion is doing.
If we did not have this sort of arrangement, do you think we could have got $5 million for flood rehabilitation and $7-5 million for rebuilding the dikes in the Fraser, or $1-2 million for hospital grants or $1-5 million on health grants?
"I say it is well worthwhile."
Then, for fear that Premier Johnson and Mr. Anscomb may have been misquoted, I wrote to the premier in this connection, a letter to which I received on March 17 the following reply:
I have for acknowledgment your letter of March 15 and note your desire for copies of the speeches made by Mr. Anscomb and myself in connection with the debate on dominion-provincial tax agreement. This matter, as you perhaps are aware, came up during the discussion on the Minister of Finance's vote in committee of supply. I spoke extempore, consequently, I have no copy of the speech and as you know we do not keep a Hansard. However, I saw the press reports of the debate and may say that they were fairly representative of what was actually said.
Hon. members will now understand the desperate predicament of the hon. member for Kamloops in deciding which of these two leaders he should be loyal to. If, as may well happen, we have the provincial and federal elections at the same time in British Columbia, he will have to take two different roles. If he is supporting a federal Conservative candidate, "the tax agreement is a vile and iniquitous deal"; if he is supporting a provincial Conservative candidate, "the tax agreement is well worth while"-a real Jekyll and Hyde role.

He was in an extremely difficult position in criticizing this budget, not just because of the fact that he knew that the budget had been so warmly welcomed by the people of Canada, but also because of the very sincere compliment paid earlier by his chief lieutenant, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Perhaps I am inaccurate in referring to him as chief lieutenant, for he very often

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair appears to be captain, too. However, I believe the house will agree that the C.C.F. has no more careful student of parliamentary history, customs and procedure, and his studious and considered opinions are always highly regarded by members of all parties in the house.
Therefore it is especially noteworthy that this distinguished student of parliamentary history should have made so striking an observation as he did as reported at page 1803 of Hansard. The Minister of Finance was approaching the end of his long and welcome list of tax removals and tax reductions when the well-informed member for Winnipeg North Centre asked him, with genuine admiration in his voice:

DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) I was reminded of the old saying of whistling to keep up your courage. I think many people have failed to realize that this is a world of failing markets. I am sorry the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and his parliamentary assistant are not here tonight because I wanted to point out some of the things that are happening to our markets. When our farmers lose their markets it will mean that the rest of the people will be in a serious situation. A lot of people have incomes of $3,800 a year, but they do not have the expenditures that farmers have. A gross income of $3,800 is a very small amount of money when farm expenses are considered. During the weeks that have passed since the budget was introduced, and in the days previous to its introduction, we heard it referred to as a sunshine budget. Let me tell you that in the country the sunshine budget has been eclipsed by the clouds of reality. People have found out that it does not mean as much as they thought it did on the night it was delivered. In fact the next morning I said to the first two people I met, "You had better smile this morning; your taxes are down." They said, "not enough." I suppose never in Canada's history has a budget died so quickly. We find thousands of people who are not helped at all, people on fixed incomes, on pensions, widows with children trying to maintain homes, low income groups. Farmers find that their costs are up and their incomes are down because prices for their products are down.
It has been referred to before, but I want to recall again the words of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King) who referred to the sales tax as iniquitous and said that it pressed alike on the rich and the

The Budget-Mr. H. O. White poor. We find that under this budget widows purchasing annuities to provide pensions for their old age are taxed for so doing.
Coming events cast their shadows before. That has been said many times, and the election cycle that has been referred to by others certainly had some influence on the budget. We heard much about taxing in times of prosperity and reducing the debt so that when more difficult times came taxes would not be as high. During the past three years the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) saw fit to extract from the people $1,600 million more than was necessary to carry on the business of the country, but we find that last year interest payments were $8 million greater than in 1947. I and a good many others are wondering what he did with the $1,600 million he took away from us. It certainly was not used for the purpose we were led to believe that it would be used for. How much does this overtaxation amount to? For a family of five it amounts to $250. That is overtaxation, not total taxation; it is just that much more than they should have taken.
In the budget no consideration was given to the needs of the blind people. Four million dollars was provided for television for people who can see; but for the small minority who are blind, and who have no political influence in the country, not a cent is provided. The government also failed to implement in full the promises made to the delegations that came to Ottawa regarding cattle which reacted to tuberculin tests.
I want to refer again to the $4 million set aside for television. That $4 million is lost and will n.ever be regained. It will take another $25 million to follow it up, although that work could be well done by private companies without one cent of cost to the taxpayers. I think that is a terrible waste of the people's money at the present time.
The estimates reveal no economy. As closely as I can figure from the estimates tabled, we are estimating for an expenditure of $2,127 million, and that is up $27 million from the year before. Savings have been effected in the wrong places. I find that the estimates of the Department of Labour are down $2 million, those of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply are down $69 million, and those of the Department of Agriculture are down $10 million. Practically all other departments are up. The Minister of Finance could have taken at least one hand out of the taxpayers' pockets.
The government is budgeting for a surplus of $87 million in the coming year, but what are the facts? The $4 million for television that I mentioned is a total loss. The $55 million for Newfoundland was not mentioned. The $40 million deficit of the C.N.R. was not

mentioned, and the loss of our foreign markets was not mentioned. We will have deficits there. There will be people who have paid income tax in past years but who will not pay income tax in the years that lie ahead. Adding those items, and without taking into consideration the loss of markets, there is $99 million that is not accounted for. If my arithmetic is anywhere near correct, we will have a deficit of at least $12 million. Oh what a tangled web we weave!
I hold in my hand two clippings from the London Free Press. The heading on the first is:
Canada's trade balance records sharp decline. Imports rise; sales abroad show slump.
What are the facts? These figures are from the dominion bureau of statistics. I am quoting from the London Free Press of April 15, 1949. The article reads in part:
Reporting monthly trade totals, the bureau of statistics disclosed today that the favourable balance -the excess of exports over imports-fell to $1,200,000 in February from $15,200,000 in January and $28,100,000 in February, 1948.
If these figures are not revealing as to the state of Canada's trade abroad I do not know what is. They reveal that we are in a much more desperate situation than the government is prepared to admit. There is another reference I wish to make to the London Free Press of April 22, 1949. The article refers to a new deal in trade and money as being imperative. It reads in part:
Because of the rigid "dollar standard," Canada of all her food agreements with the United Kingdom has left but wheat, bacon, cheese and eggs, all of them considerably reduced. Meanwhile the United Kingdom has turned elsewhere for the products that Canada used to provide. The situation is far from satisfactory. But the day rapidly is approaching when a "new deal" in money mechanics and trade will be forced upon Canada, the United States and the sterling area.
I suppose one should not fail to mention the North Atlantic security pact, that historic document which was signed previous to the Easter recess. I want to refer to the able presentation of the needs, aims and desires of the nations that are signatories to that pact, the able presentation by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and the reply of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I want to point out now one thing that happened. My friends to the left, the C.C.F., never fail to point out the shortcomings of the Progressive Conservative party, and sometimes refer to its members being absent, but eleven of their party failed to vote on the North Atlantic security pact. As you will recall, most of them were in the city of Ottawa, but were not in their seats in the house.
