speechtext:
I want to point out that there have been other pacts in the past which have failed, as my leader pointed out in his speech on another occasion. They failed because they were not made living, workable, vital realities. The Atlantic pact is a military alliance, a political unity against an apparent common foe. But more important than these considerations is the fact that there should be also economic co-operation between the nations who are signatories to this pact, so that trade may flow both backward and forward more freely than it has in the past. Before it closes, the commonwealth conference now coming to an end should take into consideration the facts I have pointed out, and find a way to help trade. Otherwise the pact and many other things we hold dear may perish. The North Atlantic family of nations must bring into being a more convertible currency or suffer disaster. Not many years ago we read of Willkie's one world. That world has been split in two; but worse still is the fact that the western half of that now divided world is again split, and we find ourselves in a peculiar position. I quote again from the London Free Press of March 25:
Caught as we are with one foot in the sterling area and the other in the dollar area we are in a precarious position.
I doubt if we can long permit international trade organizations and international monetary funds, both the result of socialist planning, to go on strangling trade. We find that these economic planners are providing for a planned scarcity, not for the planned plenty they talked about. In further reference to Canada's dwindling trade I want to quote also from the Ottawa Journal of December 14:
Having accepted fixed prices, controlled marketing, and the oft-repeated promise of long-term food contracts with the United Kingdom, Canadian farmers suddenly find that, with the lone exception of the cheese contract, these food agreements are about as firm as tissue paper. Britain doesn't even want our bacon, or at least cannot pay for it in any coin we will accept. Urged for years to produce in abundance, the Canadian farmer now finds that about the only assured market is the domestic one-which cannot absorb all he can produce.
The Budget-Mr. H. O. White
Canada's dwindling trade can be compared to the extent of our participation in the Berlin air lift; nothing at all. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) or his parliamentary assistant (Mr. McCubbin) had been in the house this evening I wanted to deal particularly with Bill No. 82, the marketing act. The only thing wrong with it is that it is fourteen years late. For years the farmers have been asking for this legislation, and now it has come too late to do them any good. I am reminded of someone who has bought an expensive machine. He knows nothing about it, but he has fooled with it until it will no longer work. Then he says, "This will not work. I will give it back to you". That is the situation as far as Canada's markets are concerned. Now that we have lost them the government are giving us the means to handle them. Hon. members will remember that early in the session, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) went to Washington, there was an article in the Ottawa Journal saying that Mr. St. Laurent was after Mr. Truman's secret, that there was some similarity between his position and that of Mr. Truman. I can tell the Prime Minister and the members of the government how Mr. Truman won his election. He gave the farmers of the United States a fair, square deal, and that is more than can be said for this administration.
The Marshall plan is also throttling our trade, for this reason. The United States produces many of the same products we produce; and when these things are declared surplus in the United States, ECA dollars are no longer available to purchase the Canadian surpluses. We have some Canadian products that have not been declared surplus, and I have in mind particularly beans and honey; but they point out to us very carefully that if we offer beans and honey for sale abroad they will declare those products surplus, so the effect will be the same. As the Financial Post says, we have put a picket fence around the dollar world.
I want to say a word or two also about the Agricultural Prices Support Act, which in 1945 was heralded as an election winner. Farmers supported the government because of that act, but what has it become in 1949? It is a millstone around the neck of the government. I have a copy of that act before me, and it is not much better than a scrap of paper. I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, how and why that is so. On March 15, 1949, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in reply to a question I asked concerning a floor price for flax, said in part at page 1472 of Hansard:
Under the circumstances the government is not prepared to encourage the production of oilseeds by establishing support prices for 1949-50.

The Budget-Mr. H. O. White
The government announced that $400,000 had been set aside to support the price of beans, and a day or so before the house adjourned it was announced that some five million pounds of honey would be bought in order to support the price of that commodity. A pattern has been set in the administration of the Agricultural Prices Support Act for the days that lie ahead. As far as flax is concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said there is no market for it, so they are not going to support it; and they could do the same thing for any other commodity the farmers produce. That is not a very heartening outlook for Canadian farmers in the production years ahead. Let us look at the position with respect to beans. We produce each year about 1,250,000 bushels of beans. Ordinarily we consume one million bushels, so 250,000 bushels are left. The government has set aside $400,000 to support the price. Of that total some $200,000 was used to purchase beans at the floor price for shipment to Israel. That means $200,000 is left to support the price of 200,000 bushels of beans, or at the rate of a dollar a bushel. You might as well try to prop open a barn door with a willow wand as to support the price of 200,000 bushels of beans with $200,000. The same thing applies to five million pounds of honey which are to be purchased. We have a surplus of about fifteen million pounds, and taking five million pounds off the market will not help a great deal. The government should have said they would take every pound of honey offered at Montreal at the price they quoted. They might not have obtained much more than five million pounds because Canadians then would have realized that was the price. But as it is, it does not mean a great deal. So while the beekeepers were hopeful for the time being, the final actual result is that they are still fearful of what is going to happen in the days ahead.
I am just going to point out to the government that they will have to make this floor price program work in the Agricultural Prices Support Act or perish in the attempt. They will never have another opportunity. It is another case of too little and too late.
Right here I also want to point out that it was one of the government's agencies, the dominion bureau of statistics, that helped to get the Canadian farmers and particularly the beekeepers in the position in which they find themselves at the moment. They reported that Canada's crop of honey was the biggest in history and that prices would go down. If the bureau of statistics had said that labour is plentiful and that the price of labour is going down, all the labour organizations in the country would have been down the government's throat, and rightly so. But they could do this to the farmers and the producers of

food, and nothing was said. The bureau of statistics should report figures but they should not predict what is going to happen because of them. They could have said that there is only four pounds per person of honey produced in Canada this year, and it probably would all have been consumed and it would not have cost the government this amount of money it is now going to cost.
At the same time, this same government allowed the importation of two million pounds of inferior honey from foreign lands and now we are obliged to turn around and buy it, ship it out and lose the money.
The export of food products abroad is similar to the export of unemployment. So long as you keep our people busy exporting their products, then we are going to have a market for the things that Canadians produce. We should arrange our agricultural economy so as to make use of our resources of men, labour and soil. This has been done in industry and could be done in agriculture. We are importing many things that could be grown in Canada by Canadian labour, and we would not be sending Canadian dollars abroad to buy them. The importation of goods from abroad is equivalent to the importation of unemployment.
Mr. Graham Towers, in a speech in Vancouver, as reported in the Financial Post of March 26, outlined five ways in which we could overcome our United Kingdom trade difficulties; and by the way, the British market is a traditional market for some of our farm products. He suggested that sales could be improved in the United Kingdom by accepting sterling. I would suggest that many of our farm products, honey included, could be handled in this way, that these goods could be bought and could be shipped to Britain, that Canada would take payment in British sterling and, instead of bringing the sterling out of the country, would invest it in British securities maturing in ten or fifteen years time, and pay the Canadian farmer what it was worth, and later withdraw those funds. I am not taking over all on my own. In the speech that Mr. Graham Towers made, he suggested that was one way that this difficulty could be handled.
I am going to go back for a moment to agricultural price floors. I want to point out to the government that they were zealous in enforcing price ceilings. Many times we read in the press that some merchant was haled into court and fined because his price was half a cent, one cent or a few cents above the price ceiling. But the government are not so zealous to enforce the floors. They certainly wait a long time before they put them into action. Do not think for one moment that the people throughout Canada

who suffered under the price ceilings are not going to realize the implication of this fact. I am going to point out to the government that if they put the skids under agriculture, agriculture will put the skids under the government and they have plenty of oleomargarine and butter with which to do it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before coming to the budget speech, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make reference to a remark which was made by the speaker who has just taken his seat. I am prompted to make this remark because he refused to answer a question which was put to him by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight). He referred to this group as being delinquent, so to speak, when, on the vote on the motion pertaining to the Atlantic pact, there were eleven members from this party absent. He made no reference to the absence of members from his own party or of members of the Liberal party or of any other party. He made no reference to the circumstances under which this vote was taken. According to the amended rules, this house must adjourn at ten-thirty; and about twenty minutes after ten o'clock, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) interrupted the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and asked for unanimous consent of the house to sit after ten-thirty. A great many members were not present in the house at that time, as happens perhaps every day. No one expected to vote, and not only C.C.F.'ers but Progressive Conservatives and Liberals left the chamber and were not present in the house when the division bells rang.
In order to put the records straight, may I say that there were eleven C.C.F. members absent, which amounts to 34 per cent of our membership in this house. There were twenty-four Progressive Conservatives absent, which amounts to 35 per cent of their membership in this house and there were fifty-two Liberals absent which amounts to 42 per cent of their membership in this house. And I think there were five Social Crediters absent, which amounts to thirty-eight per cent of their membership in this house. I think it was most unfair for the hon. member who has just taken his seat to make reference to this matter.
Coming to the budget speech, I may say that I am not quite as enthusiastic about this budget as is the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), who finished his speech about half an hour ago. In spite of the atmosphere of curious expectancy surrounding the budget speech on the day that the minister delivered it in this house, I find that it was no surprise to anyone in this country. It certainly was no surprise to me. We all had expected these reductions, which
The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke were only due to the people of Canada. It has been mentioned by the financial critic of the official opposition that it was a bribery or election budget. I would say this. The people of Canada in an election year expect an election budget, and I would say that they expected an election budget this year. I think that they were somewhat disappointed after the first glamour had worn off.
Of course there is some relief, and I give the minister credit for giving us that relief. While I think some of my constituents will be very glad of the relief that has been given, yet there is also a great disappointment. I had expected even from this government some fiscal change which would have had an influence in reducing the high cost of living, while at the same time maintaining the high level of income which this government must collect in order to carry on the business of the country. In spite of the minister's reassuring words about the leveling off of the cost of living index, I might tell him that the high cost of living is still a very burning issue among the people out in the country-at least it is in my constituency.
One of the things which would have had the desirable effect of reducing the cost of living is the abolition of the sales tax on the necessities of life. At the same time it would have given some relief to that large class of our people whose income is below the income tax level as it stood before the minister's budget speech was delivered. There are many of these people.
Someone referred to this budget as a Santa Claus budget. I think that is a correct description. As you know, Santa Claus is noted for being more generous in places where he would not need to be so generous. If the sales tax on the necessities of life had been abolished, it would have necessitated the enactment of some safeguards, controls so to speak, so that business would not absorb the reduction instead of passing it on to the benefit of the consumer. We have an example in point. The abolition of the tax on travel, both by air and by rail, is not being passed on to the consumer. It has been absorbed by the transportation companies. Therefore the public has received no benefit from the abolition of this tax. The immediate future will show whether or not the people will receive the benefit of other taxes which were abolished or reduced in the provisions contained in the budget. Perhaps we shall see in a few months' time that these reductions in taxation have been absorbed by business. I hope not. We shall see whether the public will get the benefit of the minister's efforts, because the government has divested itself of the power to control such matters.

The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke
I spoke about those of our fellow Canadians whose income is below the level of the lowest income tax bracket before the budget was delivered. It has already been pointed out that the lot of these people has not been assisted by the budget and there are a great many of them. As a matter of fact their lot has been made more burdensome by virtue of the government's action in abolishing the subsidies on flour, which has already caused a rise in the price of bread.
However, apart from this bad feature which has placed a burden on the low income groups of our population, I am really surprised that the sales tax was not abolished altogether or at least considerably reduced with respect to the necessities of life and the implements of primary production used by our farmers and fishermen. Sales tax is indirect taxation, and that form of taxation is called pernicious and obnoxious in the dictionary of liberalism; at least, that is what I was taught when I first absorbed the elementary principles of liberalism, namely, that indirect taxation on the necessities of life and on the tools of primary production was anathema to Liberals. I recall those times years ago when I was an ardent supporter of liberalism, and when I supported many Liberal candidates for parliament and for the legislature, and when I talked myself hoarse on the inequity and the injustice of indirect taxation. I would have thought that the Liberal party, which poses as the custodian of liberalism, now that financial conditions are a bit easier, would have jumped at the opportunity to revert to one of the basic principles of liberalism and obliterated this obnoxious tax, at least as far as it affects the necessities of life and the implements of production.
According to the statement appended to the minister's speech, the sales tax yielded $390 million in the last fiscal year. I feel of course that you cannot just abolish a tax such as that unless there is an alternative source of revenue, or unless you can economize to that extent. In view of the precarious position in which we are at the present time, I have no suggestion as to where we can economize to the extent of at least $400 million, and therefore we must look to another source of revenue. My hon. friends of the Conservative party are denouncing the sales tax as strongly as we do in this group, but so far I cannot recall their having made any suggestion as to where the additional revenue is to come from if the government should abolish or reduce the tax at least on the necessities of life. I would suggest that the reimposition of the excess profits tax would supply the needed revenue. It should be a tax somewhat similar to the tax which we abolished a few years ago, but not based so much upon a standard

profit as upon returns on investments. The government would have ample justification for the reimposition of that tax in view of the report of the parliamentary committee on prices which recommended the imposition of a tax on unreasonable profits. I do not care whether you call such a tax an excess profits tax or a tax on unreasonable profits. To me it means the same thing.
In studying the evidence that was taken before it, the prices committee were, in my opinion, justified in recommending the imposition of a tax on unreasonable profits. No doubt there are, and there were, many decent businessmen who realized the seriousness of the responsibilities which they have and who, I believe, were earnest in their endeavour to prevent a condition of inflation, and they were satisfied with reasonable profits. But the evidence before the prices committee showed that there are a great many irresponsible firms which took full advantage of the situation arising out of the decontrol policy of the government and out of the austerity program which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) put before this house at the last session of parliament, and they made what I call unreasonable profits. They made unreasonable profits and they should be taxed.
If one reads the evidence, I think any reasonable man will agree that the committee's recommendation was in line with the evidence, and that a recommendation of such a tax on unreasonable profits would have been justified. I maintain it would have been well received by the large majority of the people in Canada. A tax such as this alone would, I believe, have a beneficial effect upon the whole prices structure, and would have had the tendency to prevent unscrupulous traders from taking advantage of the situation in which we find ourselves in this country. Apart from this, I think that the tax would have taken care of the loss of revenue from the sales tax which would have resulted if this tax had been abolished. I do not think that such a tax on unreasonable profits would have been too great a burden on industry and business. I have no statistics, but from reading the financial pages of the daily press, and from reading these interesting articles and items in the financial press, it would appear that, so far as business is concerned, profits of all corporations seem to be still on the upgrade, and seem to be mounting-even though, of course, there is the odd firm which reports a set-back, so far as profits are concerned.
I think everyone agrees that corporation profits are still on the upgrade, and I submit that this is where the additional money should have come from. Therefore I say that

the failure of the government to abolish or at least to reduce the sales tax on the necessities of life and the implements of primary production has been a great disappointment to the majority of the people because, first of all, they have given no relief to a large group of our people who really need relief more than any other group and, secondly, they have failed to revert to one of the basic principles of liberalism, of which they claim to be the champions.
A great deal has been said in praise of this budget by speakers supporting the government, and they are joyous because of the reduction of our national debt. For instance, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) mentioned twice this evening that our national debt had been reduced by $1,600 million. I should like to show that this is not quite correct, and I do not think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made any such statement. It is said the surpluses in the last three years which amount roughly to $1,600 million have been used to reduce our national debt and, as a matter of fact, that is the impression that is prevalent in the country, namely that the national debt has been reduced through this so-called cyclical budgeting in the last three years by this impressive sum of $1,600 million. As I said a moment ago, the hon. member for Vancouver North made that assertion again this evening.
I claim that this is not true. It is rather difficult to figure out the actual amount from the tables which I have at hand; but in 1947 the funded debt of Canada was, roughly, $16,500 million, according to the balance sheet tabled with the budget speech in that year; and at the end of March, 1949, the funded debt of Canada is $15,500 million, according to the statement tabled with the minister's budget speech on March 22, and appended to Hansard of that date.
It seems to me that the reduction of the funded debt was just a little over one billion dollars, and not over $1,600 million, as claimed by the hon. member for Vancouver North.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member wishes to be fair. The reduction of $1,625 million was in Canada's net debt.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am referring to the funded debt; I shall come to the net debt later. It seems to me that the reduction of the funded debt was just a little over one billion dollars, and that there is a difference of $600 million. I am referring to the funded debt, while the minister is referring to the net debt.
The net debt has of course been reduced and our position in that respect has been improved. But that is only after crediting 29087-162J
The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke against the gross debt the loans which we have made to our customers to purchase our surplus products in the last three years. Because of the doubt as to the repayment of these assets-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one does my hon. friend think will not be repaid?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not say they will not be repaid. But I say, as we said in 1947 when these loans were made, that there is a doubt. I hope they will all be paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The country which has the most has never repudiated her debts, so far as I know.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope they will all be repaid. I repeat that I hope the loans which we made to these countries will all be repaid. At the present time however we owe this money. We took it from the taxpayers, because our loans to those countries have been increased by $600 million in the last three years. I believe the minister will confirm that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More than that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not according to the table; it is just approximately $600 million; and that is just about the same amount as the difference between the reduction in the net debt and the reduction in the gross debt.
Mind you, I make no objection to this. But the news got out to the country that we had decreased our debt by $1,600 million. Our net debt, yes; but not our funded debt. Our funded debt has been reduced by only about one billion dollars. The minister himself does not claim credit for that. He does not claim that all the surplus he had this year was applied in the reduction of the funded debt. At page 1793 of Hansard is the minister's statement showing the net reduction in funded debt of $472 million, less the increase in the United States funded debt, which we owe to the United States, of $100 million, leaving a net reduction in funded debt of $372 million, as against a surplus of $650 million.
So much for that point. The most important part of the minister's speech, to my mind, deals with our general economic situation, which is tied up so closely with our overseas trade. The minister was most interesting in his discourse respecting this situation. While he points out all the difficulties now confronting us, and which are in prospect for the future, he seems to offer no solution. I shall quote briefly from his speech at pages 1788 and 1789 of Hansard. In what I shall quote I do not believe the fact of lifting these quotations from their context

The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke will result in any misrepresentation of what the minister said. These are his words:
In the light of all these adverse conditions, our -export trade has stood up relatively well but we cannot be satisfied with its present situation or immediate prospects. We must seek improvement . . .
We must search for adjustments . . .
We must develop alternative outlets . . .
We must persevere in working out the constructive solution through trade agreements on a wide and indiscriminatory basis, and by other measures of a basic character that will assist those countries that buy from us to find dollar markets for their own exports in order that they may pay for what they would rightly like to get from us.
I cannot see any solution in this, except that perseverance on our part is the only solution.
Then he speaks of the solution of this problem which has been suggested by this group on several occasions in the present session, when we have urged that the government should try to embark upon a policy of barter deals. He admits in his speech that it is attempting to consider such deals, but he rejects the idea, as set out in his speech in these words:
In the first place, most of our trade takes place with the United States, both export and import, and we cannot deal that way there . . . Secondly, we are not in a good bargaining position to make successful bilateral deals . . . The normal and healthy pattern of our trade is triangular or multilateral.
It seems to me that the minister is trying to go back to international trade as it existed before the two wars. If we look at the whole world I think we must realize that the old concept of world trade is gone. I think history is evidence that the world does not go back, that it progresses. We have no control over the method that our customers or our potential customers might prefer to use in carrying on world trade and it seems to me that we have to learn that lesson if we want to trade. The situation today is not the same as it was before the wars when all trade rolled along in that eternal triangle about which we heard so much when we discussed the bill to deal with the prohibition and restriction of imports last year. There was that old triangular proposition when Great Britain was the clearing house for international trade. Our great neighbour to the south has presumed to take up the task where Britain left off through force of circumstances, not that she wished it or willed it. However, it seems to me that our great neighbour to the south is not measuring up to the task.
Either the United States must imitate Britain or the international bank or the monetary fund must be substantially changed so that foreign trade such as the minister likes to envision can be carried on smoothly without the continual headache of international balances and the convertibility of

currency. I maintain that we are not going backward to pre-war standards but are progressing and must adjust our conditions and policies accordingly.
A very interesting article appeared in Foreign Trade of March 19, a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The title of this article is, "World trade affected by efforts of many countries to balance dollar accounts". Much of the article is copied from the last report of the foreign exchange control board made to the minister and tabled in this house. However, the article goes somewhat further than the report and submits the main types of solution. I should like to quote the pertinent paragraph in the article which refers to the very situation I have been discussing during the past few minutes. This reads as follows:
With the growing severity of import restrictions imposed by many countries, an increasing number of cases have arisen where Canadian exporters find it impossible to sell goods on the prescribed terms of payment. In these cases, alternative proposals for payment are sometimes made by foreign buyers and, where they are acceptable to the Canadian exporters, the foreign exchange control board has indicated its readiness to consider applications for the necessary permits. The following are the main types of case which warrant consideration:
(a)	Exports for payment in the appropriate currencies, but where payment is to be deferred beyond the normal six-month period.
(b)	Exports to previously established markets for payments in "blocked" foreign currencies, i.e., foreign currencies which are not freely convertible into United States dollars or sterling.
(c)	Exports to non-sterling area countries for payment in sterling, where the United Kingdom exchange control authorities are prepared to authorize the foreign importer to transfer the sterling to the Canadian exporter.
(d)	Exports to be paid for by the acceptance of goods of equivalent value.
That article advocates a trial of the very things that we have been advocating in this house since the session opened in January, that we try to make barter deals with our customers as is being done by other countries. This article suggests that a means of improving our foreign trade might be the trying out of exports to be paid for by the acceptance of goods of equivalent value. The minister rejected this in the following words, and I quote from Hansard at page 1788:
. . . the application of a policy of barter, bilateral deals and discrimination requires widespread governmental control of private trade, and even the extending of trade by agencies of the government itself. Deals of this sort would require a multiplication of import controls, export controls, licences, and permits. It is about to lead to more government buying and selling, frequently involving subsidies and trading losses. This may fit into the philosophy of governments prevailing in some other countries, but most Canadians don't like controls and don't want their government getting deeper and deeper into import and export business.
I think the minister is a bit too pessimistic when he foresees the objectionable features of

these deals. However, he made this pertinent observation and I quote him again:
This may fit into the philosophy of governments prevailing in other countries.
That is exactly my point. We have no control over those other governments, but if they are our potential customers I think we should fit in our policies with their policies in order that we might trade and survive. If one studies and follows this excellent periodical Foreign Trade one must come to the conclusion that almost every country in the world except Canada and the United States controls its international trade in this or a similar manner. They are forced to do so. They are forced to form customs unions like that about to be formed in the near future by France and Italy.
In the March 26 issue of Foreign Trade we read that a five-man commercial mission left Peru for London early in March at the invitation of the British government to discuss ways and means by which exports from Britain to Peru could be increased. Almost every week similar items pertaining to world trade and to barter deals, as we call them, are to be found in Foreign Trade and also in the daily press. This is all done with the idea of getting world trade moving because it will not move under the old system.
It has been mentioned in the house that co-operatives and even private traders have endeavoured to conclude deals in foreign countries for the exchange of goods, as is suggested in Foreign Trade of March 19. I cannot see why, without any great interference on the part of the government, organizations such as co-operatives or even private traders could not make deals of this sort. I think it is worth a trial. The government has elaborate machinery in the Department of Trade and Commerce, which I think is an excellent department. There are trade commissioners spread over the face of the globe and we also have the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The machinery is there whereby the government could assist co-operatives, provincial governments if you like, private traders or any person to make barter deals with some of these countries which do not trade today in any other way.
I realize of course that there is the nondiscriminatory principle of the Geneva agreement, but that agreement has many escape clauses. Those escape clauses are being taken advantage of today by almost every country that signed the treaty except Canada and the United States, I was going to say. Even in the United States they have taken some advantage of the escape clause I mentioned a year ago.
The Geneva agreement is trying to take us back to pre-war conditions, and while I am
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore generally in accord with its provisions and its aims, since I was taught that free trade is the proper way to carry on world trade,
I believe that, while an agreement like that would have worked wonderfully twenty-five years ago, it will not do today what its sponsors hope it will. Members of the Atlantic union being pledged to economic co-operation are likely to succeed more satisfactorily among themselves, and I believe that the members who signed the Atlantic pact will have more success by economic co-operation, even if they should leave out Canada and the United States, as they are doing at the present time. I think we in Canada cannot afford to stand aside. I think we must make a trial in view of the prospects for foreign trade at the present time, and that some consideration should be given by the government to the question of barter deals especially since a trial seems to be recommended in the article on foreign trade that I have just read.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For a
few moments I desire to direct the attention of the house to another type of subject. World war I veteran, Lieutenant Stuart Brown entered Shaughnessy hospital to be treated for neurasthenia and gunshot wounds, a disability that would be pensionable if proven to exist. I should like to have the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), or anyone else who feels competent to perform the task, find out and tell the house and the country who are the men whose signatures committed Lieutenant Stuart Brown from Shaughnessy hospital to Essondale insane asylum, thereby nullifying Lieutenant Brown's title to pension.
While they are about it I should also like them to say who are the men whose signatures later committed world war I veteran Brown to Colquitz mental home where at that time only the permanently and criminally insane were lodged. All being well, I shall have more to say about Colquitz when and if at some future time I speak again concerning Lieutenant Brown. I believe the house and the country would like to know upon whose orders or consent or acquiescence these outrages were committed against veteran Brown, a free Canadian with no criminal record, a man sane then, sane ever since then, and sane now. I think every normal Canadian would also like to know who it was who wrote into veteran Brown's record two monstrous falsehoods, first that veteran Brown had been in an asylum prior to the war, and second that veteran Brown had been arrested and charged with an offence against children, these falsehoods never having had the slightest foundation in fact; the existence of these falsehoods in his records being utterly unknown to veteran Brown until a legion committee examining his records later found them there;

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore and these falsehoods since having been established as falsehoods beyond the slightest peradventure of doubt.
I must say that I find this account of what happened to veteran Brown incomprehensible and utterly inconceivable, but apparently the thing has happened right here in Canada. The house and the country are entitled to know, and should know without further delay, what steps, if any, any government department has taken to bring to justice the perpetrators of these reprehensible crimes against veteran Brown. We are entitled to know also what machinery the government has set up to discover, liberate and recompense the scores of similar helpless victims probably at present languishing in living graves in insane asylum cells across Canada.
Members who have given some attention to the Thomas Harvey case, which I had the honour of bringing to the notice of the house some weeks ago, will be interested to know that veteran Thomas Harvey told me-almost the first thing he said when he had given his own submission-that there was another man in the insane asylum where he was who was just as sane as anyone could be, and who had been languishing there for twenty-five years.
Another question that ought to be answered -and whatever red tape it is necessary to cut in order to answer it ought to be cut forthwith- is: What adequate measures has any department of the government taken to render impossible the occurrence of like abominations in the future? What steps has the government taken to remove from veteran Brown's record the two falsehoods? It is bad enough if a man's own deeds are recorded in his record. Few people ever succeed in living through life with the record of complete angels. Their own slips are sufficient, but to have a man in the employ of any department of the government free to write with impunity absolute and utter falsehoods into the record of a man, and to have that go by unpunished and unrectified, is a thing which I must say leaves one virtually speechless in contemplation thereof.
I should like to read for the benefit of the members of the house and of the people of the country some quotations from veteran Stuart Brown's own account of his experiences, as the account appears in the January 8, 1949, issue of the Vancouver Sunday Sun magazine.
I would commend this article to everyone who has a heart for the honour of Canada. It appears in three issues of the paper I have mentioned. Stuart Brown is speaking and the article is called, "They put me in Essondale." The article reads:
I was confined four years to lunatic asylums in British Columbia, put there by persons with rotten motives. Psychiatrists and those who know me well said I was sane then. They say I am sane now. I

had no criminal record, still have none. But a record of one of the worst sorts of conviction was set down against me, presumably to help frame up my consignment to the asylum.
Also it was recorded that I had been in asylum. I had not.
My removal from Shaughnessy hospital to Essondale was effected by two doctors putting their signatures to the necessary document. I had no recourse.
If I had not finally escaped, and from the wilds of Vancouver island, where I lived on frozen apples and, before being recaptured, pencilled an, urgent letter to Lord Tweedsmuir, then governor general of Canada, I'd probably be locked up yet in dismal Colquitz prison asylum near Victoria.
And by the time I had died there, if granted threescore years and ten, my maintenance, at even $600 a year, would have cost taxpayers about $20,000.
But, thank God, Lord Tweedsmuir ordered an investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and I am free. Yet I have had no recompense. And, according to the record, I am still insane.
I move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker, and I shall go on with these remarks tomorrow.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

He said: Mr. Speaker, earlier in the day the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) asked if I would indicate the further business to be brought before the house prior to the end of the session. I think it only fair that I should say to the house at this time, in announcing the business for tomorrow, that I have placed a notice on Votes and Proceedings to take Wednesday for government business, and asking that on Wednesday the house continue to sit after dinner; also asking that the house sit from eleven o'clock to one o'clock on Thursday morning and each day thereafter to the end of the session. That would leave the usual hour tomorrow and Friday for private and public bills, in the order in which they appear on the order paper. In this motion I am also moving that standing order 28 be not applied on Thursday. That is the standing order which provides that the Speaker leaves the chair without question put. For reasons I shall give in a moment, we are asking that this standing order be suspended so that grievances may be brought up on Thursday when the motion is made that the Speaker leave the chair.
All hon. members know there must be a general election within the next year, and there are a good many reasons why one should be held earlier than that. In the first place there has been a change in the leadership of the government since the general election of 1945; and it has always been my view that I should attempt to get from the people, at as early a date as possible, confirmation of what has been done.

When I became Prime Minister in November of last year certain developments were in process which could not be interrupted without serious prejudice to the interests of our own country, and perhaps to wider interests still. I refer to the negotiations then in progress with the delegation from Newfoundland, and to the discussions being carried on at that time in Washington respecting the North Atlantic security pact. Once the agreement with Newfoundland was signed on December 11, it provided that the union should be concluded on March 31, and it was essential to hold a session of parliament in order to approve the agreement. In the opinion of the government it was also essential to deal with certain emergency legislation which otherwise would have expired within two months after the opening of the session or on March 31 last, whichever date was the earlier. It was also felt that the people of Canada would expect to have the budget presented at an early date; and it was the desire of the government, before authorizing the signature of Canada to the North Atlantic treaty, to secure the approval of parliament to the principles underlying that treaty.
All these essential steps have been taken. The union with Newfoundland has been completed. The North Atlantic treaty has been signed. The budget has been presented, and the estimates for the current fiscal year have been before parliament and the public for several weeks. My colleagues and I have reached the conclusion that no important public interest would suffer if the rest of the business forecast for the present session of parliament should be postponed until later this year. It is pretty evident that until a general election is held it will be difficult for hon. members on both sides of the house not to give a good deal of attention to the forthcoming election; and probably it would not be an exaggeration to say that already some of the debates in the house have become tinged by the approach of an election campaign.
General elections, of course, are the most mportant institution in our whole constitu-.ion, since it is through a general election that the public maintains control over the government. But it is also true that a general election campaign is necessarily disturbing to much of the ordinary activity of the community, and there seems to be a widespread feeling that there is no great advantage in prolonging such campaigns. Moreover it is perfectly clear that the holding of an election in the summer months would result in the virtual disfranchisement of a large portion of
Business of the House
the electorate who do not spend the summer in their habitual place of residence.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: Call it in June.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
The hon. member will see in a moment what I am proposing. There are many others whose seasonal activities make it very difficult for them to attend meetings or even exercise their franchise during the midsummer or harvest season.
Therefore in fairness to the people the government feels that the forthcoming election should be held either at the beginning of the summer or that it should be delayed until after the harvest season, which in many parts of Canada extends even into October.
Without wishing to reflect on anyone in the house, my colleagues and I feel that more rapid progress would be made-except such as was made today-in a session held after a general election than would be possible if the present session were continued even for two or three months. Moreover, by holding an election at an early date the people will be given an opportunity to decide to whom they wish to entrust the responsibilities of government, and to give some indication of the policies they wish to see implemented.
In view of the very considerable changes in the membership of the administration, that in itself might be thought a sufficient reason for holding an early election. But there is a much more important reason still. It is that about one-third of a million people have been added to the population of our country. There is no doubt that one of the principal reasons why the people of Newfoundland voted for union with Canada was that they wished once more to be self-governing. Since every measure adopted by the present parliament applies to Newfoundland as much as it does to the older provinces, it is desirable to take the earliest possible means of ensuring that the people of Newfoundland are represented in parliament and share, through their representatives, in making its decisions.
Of course it would have been possible to arrange for by-elections in Newfoundland immediately after March 31, but even after that had been done the newly elected members could not have taken their seats before about the end of June, and it is not probable that if we were sitting at the end of June we would continue to sit very much beyond that date. As I think there is a general desire throughout the country that there should be a general election before another session of parliament, they would have had their by-elections, there would have been dissolution, and they would have had to undergo two elections in order to send their representatives here to take part in the conduct

Business of the House
of their country's affairs, because it is theirs now as much as it is our own. Therefore the government has reached the conclusion that it is desirable from the point of view of the country to hold a general election as soon as possible.
As to the matters with which it would be desirable to deal at this time, if possible, there is this pipe lines legislation which has gone to a committee of this house and which the government would ask the house to consider as soon as the committee makes a report. Then we would continue this debate on the budget and the budget resolutions, and the legislation consequent upon these resolutions. It is hoped that that might be disposed of tomorrow or Wednesday; and immediately following the budget resolutions or, if they are not disposed of by Wednesday evening, on Thursday the Minister of Finance will move to go into committee of supply to ask for interim supply for the period required to hold an election and to bring a new parliament together. It is in order that that motion may not come under the effect of standing order 28, which provides that the Speaker leave the chair on Thursdays and Fridays without question put, that I am asking that that rule be suspended; so that if hon. members have grievances which they feel should get the consideration of the house, there will be the ordinary motion for the Speaker to leave the chair in order to go into committee of supply for the purpose of asking for interim supply for a period sufficient to take care of the necessary activities of the country in the time required to hold an election and to bring parliament together as early as convenient after the election is held.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: When will that be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Whoever has the responsibility of forming a government will have to fix the date for the session. All the Minister of Finance will ask the house to do at this time is to vote interim supply for a period that would be sufficient to hold the election and to call the new parliament at a convenient date.
I think all parties opposite us have expressed doubts at least as to the confidence of the country in the present administration. The motion now before the house on the budget resolutions is not that this house has not confidence in the government but that the people have not confidence in the government, and I think it is preferable to have the people themselves answer that question. No measures of which notice has not already been given will be proceeded with, except possibly resolutions to approve the North Atlantic treaty and the international wheat agreement, if there is time to deal with them. [Mr. St. Laurent.!
I wish to be completely frank with the house. It is the intention of the government at the end of this week to recommend to His Excellency that he dissolve this parliament.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) mentions the resolution dealing with old age pensions. Notice has already been given of that. It is included in the matters of which notice has already been given. The only matters of which notice has not already been given, and which it would be desirable to proceed with if there were time to do so, would be the resolutions approving the North Atlantic treaty and approving the international wheat agreement. The international wheat agreement, by its terms, would apply to the wheat crop year commencing on August 1, if there have been a sufficient number of ratifications deposited by that time, though for a large portion of our wheat crop for the year 1949-50 we have the United Kingdom contract. It would be, I think, desirable to have the international wheat agreement ratified by the required number of countries before the beginning of the next crop year.

speechtext: It is intended to proceed with this pipe lines legislation, then to deal with the budget until it is disposed of, if that happens before eleven o'clock on Thursday. At eleven o'clock on Thursday it is intended to ask for interim supply. Then just as soon as that has been disposed of, if we have to go back to the budget we will go back to the budget. But if not, we will deal with these other matters.

speechtext:
About four years ago, Mr. Speaker, as I stood in a position close to the one in which I now am, and when a similar announcement was made by the then Prime Minister, there was some suggestion by those on the opposite side of the house that there was not enough glee expressed in the opposition with regard to the announcement that had just been made. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that tonight I think no one can make that kind of accusation against this party. We welcome, as will the Canadian people, this government's going to the country at last. The Prime Minister has suggested that this house will be dissolved at the end of this week, if I understood his words correctly. I can readily understand the Prime Minister's position with respect to this matter. With a vote of want of confidence facing the government, with a public accounts committee about to meet and to discuss some

important matters, and with the estimates scarcely touched, I am quite sure that one can understand and perhaps sympathize with a hard-pressed Prime Minister and a weary government.
May I just say this before I resume my seat. This announcement will now give the people of Canada a chance to stand up and be counted on the straight question whether or not they want the kind of socialism which prevails in Russia, the kind of socialism which is preached by the C.C.F., or the kind of socialism that is too frequently practised by the present government in power.

I think the house and the country will appreciate the frankness of the Prime Minister tonight. As he has said, the people of Canada have the right at this time to elect a government which will be representative of all Canada, including the new province of Newfoundland. What I rose to say was that since the Prime Minister spoke of the desire of giving people such as teachers, preachers, businessmen and their families who might otherwise be away for a summer election, the opportunity of voting in their own constituencies, I was hoping that he would actually announce the date of the election so that we might know that they would have the opportunity at least before July 1.
I merely want to say that so far as we are concerned as a democratic party in this country, we believe that opportunities of this
Business of the House
kind given to the people are valuable both to the country and to this House of Commons. I am not going to indulge in a political speech. All I can say is that the people of Canada will have the choice, and I hope that they will choose wisely, progressively and well.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: They will.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: I had hoped that the government would see fit to complete the business of the session before calling an election. I do believe that the majority of the people of the country, while they do not relish continuing long in an upset, uncertain situation, appreciate having their representatives tuck in the edges and complete the year's business as it should be. However, since the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has given a lengthy series of reasons why an election should be held at the present time, I just say on behalf of our group in this house that we shall welcome the reference to the people because I believe they have the right to say whether under present circumstances the present government should be returned-

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: There is no danger of that.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: -or some other government be sent back here. There is only one thing which the Prime Minister has omitted, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) said, namely, the date of the election. Seriously, that leaves us in a kind of uncertain position. I think he has the date in mind and I am just wondering whether he will not give it to us.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
It would be quite improper for me to announce the date of the election until His Excellency has accepted the advice we shall tender at the end of the week to dissolve parliament. I said I thought that the election should be held as early as possible. If hon. members will refer to the elections act they will see that with dissolution coming at the end of the week it would leave it possible to have an election on June 27.
